commenti.body:
I'd consider looking at the original work that this film adapts, Herman Melville's "Billy Budd." 

The homoerotic aspect that you're picking up from the film is, arguably, there in the original novella -- that is at least how many critics have read it. From chapter 2, for instance:

>As the Handsome Sailor, Billy Budd’s position aboard the seventy-four was something analogous to that of a rustic beauty transplanted from the provinces and brought into competition with the highborn dames of the court. But this change of circumstances he scarce noted. As little did he observe that something about him provoked an ambiguous smile in one or two harder faces among the blue-jackets.

I think, in general, that it's important to view films as adaptations, if they are adaptations. 

>wasted potential in the alienating, hyper-masculine and colonialist institution of the military.

This is very much a key theme in the original novella. Consider this authorial aside from near the end of the story:

>True martial discipline long continued superinduces in average man a sort of impulse of docility whose operation at the official sound of command much resembles in its promptitude the effect of an instinct.

Excellent points. This story is all about homoerotic desire. In my view, Galoup's attraction towards Forrestier and Sentain is the centerpiece regardless of whose perspective the camera looks from.

I haven't read the original Billy Budd text-- would you say that the postcolonial themes of Beau Travail are present there too? I thought the contrast between the isolated group of men and their cultural/geographic surroundings was one of the more thought-provoking aspects of the movie.

The original novella is set in 1797 on a British Navy ship -- Billy Budd (the Sentain equivalent) is impressed (IE captured and forced) to work on the ship as a crewman. It can absolutely be read as a story of empire (the 18th century British Navy as a quintessential imperial symbol) and of the need to maintain discipline at all costs in imperial institutions.
I'll be sure to check it out. What's your take on the main question in my post? And what do you think of the gaze in general in Beau Travail?

I wouldn't say the locals are 'othered' by the perspective of the film, but I also don't think they're the actual viewpoint through which we're seeing the events. The film doesn't say anything about the locals themselves; they just are what they are, living their lives. 

In my eyes, the emphasis on them watching the soldiers others the soldiers as a sort of zoo type spectacle, giving the already very weird looking military exercises an alien quality. It gives the audience the proper perspective for thinking about the film in terms of colonialism.
Good points, thanks for your reply! You're right that we don't learn anything about the locals beyond the surface level. This definitely supports that they are not our camera's viewpoint.

Beyond the perspective being simply that of the filmmakers themselves, I'd say it being Galoup's view is likeliest. It's been a while since I watched the film but maybe it's decipherable through the shot choices for Sentain vs all the other soldier soldiers? I remember that moment right before the end when he's remembering his time in Djibouti we see a group shot of all of them besides Sentain.
Ooo, interesting point! I never picked up that Sentain is missing in that final shot of the group. They all look so similar haha. I'll have to go back and look.

I don’t know if everything needs to be thought of as being part of a “gaze” — that being said, I do like the reading of the entire film being Galoup’s subjective account. It certain complicates the moments we see in which Galoup is absent (are the scenes of the Djiboutians rescuing Sentain real or imagined?). And of course it’s hard to read the final scene as being anything other than Galoup’s subjectivity, although if someone has an alternate reading I’d be curious to hear it.

I agree that it requires some gymnastics to view things from anything other than Galoup's point of view, especially the ending as an externalization of his emotions. It's still interesting to imagine the story as being viewed by an anonymous non-male spectator-- someone outside the bounds of masculinity. It somehow increases the tragedy.

I think you're right on the ending. The closest I have to an alternate reading is to note how passive the camera is in that scene. Throughout the movie it's been caressing all over our characters up close, but here it takes a distant and neutral stance. I'm not totally sure what to make of it.

The long shot scale, to me, creates both physical and emotional space for Galoup’s self-expression, whereas we can use a simple commutation test to explain the still camera — if the camera had been moving in this scene, it would detract from the uniqueness of Galoup’s dance in comparison with the machinistic movements of the rest of the film.
